title: About aplastic anaemia | NHS inform
text:
About aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia is a very rare and serious bone marrow disorder that causes low blood counts. It affects around 2 people in every 1 million each year in Scotland.
What is aplastic anaemia?
Bone marrow is found within the bones and makes blood cells. In people with aplastic anaemia, bone marrow doesn’t produce blood cells normally. The production of blood cells can slow down or stop altogether. This means there’s no longer enough in the body.
There are 3 types of blood cells which all have a different role. These are:
red blood cells – important for carrying oxygen around the body
white blood cells – help fight infections, bugs and germs
platelets – stop bleeding and bruising
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust – What is aplastic anaemia?
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust has further information on what aplastic anaemia is.
Types of aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia can be:
very severe
severe
not severe
Healthcare professionals will measure the level of blood cells in your body to work out how severe your aplastic anaemia is. The fewer blood cells there are, the more severe your aplastic anaemia is likely to be.
Symptoms of aplastic anaemia
Symptoms of aplastic anaemia can vary in severity. They are caused by low blood counts, which affect red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Symptoms of aplastic anaemia can include:
fatigue
shortness of breath
headaches
chest pains
bleeding
bruising
reoccurring severe infections
Some patients also report experiencing general symptoms like:
brain fog
poor concentration
These symptoms may be caused by aplastic anaemia, different treatments, or other factors.
Diagnosing aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia is a rare cause of low blood count. If you have symptoms of a low blood count, you’ll need to have different tests to rule out other more likely reasons for it and find the exact cause.
Most patients with a low blood count will need:
blood tests
bone marrow investigations
Some people may need:
X-rays
and other scans
genetic testing
If you do have aplastic anaemia, you’ll also need tests to find out how severe it is.
Healthcare professionals will also check if you have enough vitamin B12 and folate to make blood cells. This helps to rule out other reasons for your symptoms.
Talking to healthcare professionals
It’s important that you understand what’s going on with your healthcare. This can help prepare you for any treatment or care that you need.
When you have a hospital appointment, it may help to bring someone who can provide support or take notes. You could also write down any questions before your appointment and take these with you.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust
jargon buster
can also help if there are medical words and phrases that don’t make sense to you, or make you feel uncomfortable.
Don’t be afraid to ask your healthcare team if there’s anything you’re unsure about.
Get more advice about speaking to healthcare professionals
Treatment for aplastic anaemia
If you have aplastic anaemia, your treatment will usually be managed by haematologists. They are specialist blood doctors.
Treatments will be tailored to your individual needs and can vary depending on:
how severe your aplastic anaemia is
your age
your general health
if you have any underlying health conditions
Research on treatments for aplastic anaemia is ongoing.
Further information on aplastic anaemia treatments
What causes aplastic anaemia?
In most cases, the cause of aplastic anaemia is not known. It’s seen as an unusual immune disorder, because the immune system attacks the bone marrow.
Healthcare professionals will investigate to see if there’s any underlying cause for your aplastic anaemia. For example, they’ll investigate if it could be caused by:
medication
an infection – including viral infections or hepatitis
an autoimmune condition
an inherited condition
Inherited conditions
For some people, aplastic anaemia is associated with an inherited condition. This means it runs in families.
Inherited conditions that can cause aplastic anaemia include:
Fanconi Anaemia
Dyskeratosis Congenita
Shwachman Diamond Syndrome
You may need to have a genetic test to rule out some of these causes.
Who’s most at risk of aplastic anaemia?
Aplastic anaemia can affect anyone at any age. However, it’s most common in those aged 10 to 20 years old, and those aged over 60.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust has further information on
aplastic anaemia in children and young people.
Sometimes aplastic anaemia can also be associated with another rare condition called
Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria (PNH)
.
Risks of severe aplastic anaemia
If you have aplastic anaemia and a low white blood count, you’re at a higher risk of severe infections. This means you should get medical help quickly if you become unwell.
People with aplastic anaemia who have a low platelet count are also at a higher risk of bruising and bleeding.
Common misunderstandings about aplastic anaemia
When people talk about anaemia, they often mean
iron deficiency anaemia
, but aplastic anaemia is different. It’s a serious bone marrow condition.
Aplastic anaemia is not a blood cancer, but some of the treatments may be similar. For example, you may need to be treated in hospital and some patients may need blood transfusions, medication through a drip or a bone marrow transplant.
Patients with aplastic anaemia may need to take steps to protect themselves from infections in a similar way to patients who are being treated with
chemotherapy
for their cancer.
Living with aplastic anaemia
There’s a lot of uncertainty and unpredictability surrounding aplastic anaemia. If you or someone you know has been diagnosed with aplastic anaemia, it can affect many different parts of your life.
The
Aplastic Anaemia Trust
has lots of information and support for people with aplastic anaemia, and those close to them.
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust offers services including:
a support line
– whether you’ve been diagnosed with aplastic anaemia or just have questions about it, you can use the support line to talk to someone
events online or in person
– there are various events across Scotland and the UK where you can meet other people affected by aplastic anaemia
Patient Support Facebook Group
– if you have a Facebook account, people with aplastic anaemia and their families can use it to connect with people who have experience of the condition
Find out more about living with aplastic anaemia
